extracted.intended_audience: Small law firms and SMMEs in South Africa
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and requirements for registering, prosecuting, maintaining, and enforcing trade marks, and for the subsistence, ownership, duration and enforcement of copyright and neighbouring rights in South Africa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single/Series trade mark
rubrics_metrics.description: When registering a trade mark with the CIPC, you can apply for either a single trade mark (a single distinctive mark for specific products or services falling in one class), or a series of trade marks (allowing for the registration of multiple trade marks that are variations of the core trade mark, or the same trade mark used for different but related goods or services).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select single where one distinctive mark covers the goods/services in that class; select series where you need protection for multiple variations or related uses of the core mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant (bona fide proprietor requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the bona fide proprietor of the trade mark, which is used or intended to be used in respect of the goods or services covered by the application, may apply for registration of the trade mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A licensee cannot apply in their own name. Applicant may be a natural person, juristic person (company) or a trust (if a trust, cite as 'The trustees for the time being of the (Trust name) Trust'). Any change of name/description, transfer or assignment must be applied for at CIPC with prescribed form and supporting documents and payment of official fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant address recording
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant’s address and any change of address is required to be recorded with the CIPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep applicant address current with the CIPC to ensure correspondence and formal notices reach the correct party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address for service (must be in South Africa)
rubrics_metrics.description: The physical address within South Africa where you can receive correspondence from the CIPC or third parties about your application or registered rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where applicant applies without legal representation, details should match applicant’s details. A Power of Attorney is required where application is filed on behalf of applicant. Only practising attorneys with valid Fidelity Fund Certificates may represent trade mark applicants; accountants/tax practitioners may not represent applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade mark type (verbal vs image)
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying, the applicant will select ‘verbal’ for a word mark (typed in the form) or ‘image’ for a device mark (logo, stylised word, shape, configuration) and be prompted to upload a representation of the mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the correct type to ensure the mark is represented and examined appropriately; upload clear image files for device marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of goods and services (Nice Classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: South Africa follows the Nice Classification. When filing the application you must include the class number from one of the 45 classes and the standard class heading will list the goods or services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure your goods/services fall properly within the chosen class and are correctly described. If goods/services fall in different classes, file a separate application for each class. Note: CIPC Practice Notice 1 of 2025 applies the 12th Edition of the Nice Classification for specs from 1 January 2025.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing method (FORM TM1 / CIPC IPOnline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade mark applications are filed manually by lodging form TM1, or online using the CIPC IPOnline portal, after registering as a CIPC customer and depositing funds into your CIPC customer account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose manual or online filing and ensure payment/deposit requirements are met before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing of application and application number (priority rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: On processing and payment of the application you will receive the allocated official application number, showing the application date via automated email, which proves filing and provides priority rights against later identical/similar applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trade mark is only enforceable under the Trade Marks Act once registered. You may use 'TM' at any stage; the ® symbol only after registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination (formalities and substantive)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CIPC will examine the application for compliance with formalities and perform substantive examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult CIPC Guidelines on examination for insights into filing formalities, formal examination and substantive examination; be prepared to respond to formal and substantive objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official action outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Once examined, the CIPC will issue an official action where the application is either accepted; accepted subject to amendments, modifications, conditions or limitations; or provisionally refused (Section 16(2)(a)-(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read official action carefully and respond within prosecution term to avoid lapse; acceptance subject to conditions may require amendment(s) to specification or representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution term and extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The trade mark applicant is given a three-month period to prosecute the application and formally respond to the official action. If further time is required, an extension must be requested through CIPC Online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prosecution term expires, apply to Registrar for condonation for late extension. Failure to respond before expiry (or extended term) will result in lapse of the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance and advertisement in the Patent and Trade Mark Journal
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon acceptance, the CIPC issues a Notice of Acceptance electronically. The applicant is required to submit the advertisement of acceptance electronically for publication in the Patent and Trade Mark Journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peruse the Journal consistently to look out for marks that may adversely affect your rights and monitor publication dates carefully (opposition timeline starts from publication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition period and extension mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Any interested person has three months from the publication date to file a notice of opposition; the opposition period may be extended in three-monthly intervals on application by the Opponent and agreement by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first extension is granted automatically by the Registrar; further extensions require consent of the trade mark applicant. Monitor oppositions and manage extensions strategically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration and use of the ® symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: If no opposition is encountered and the opposition term lapses, the trade mark registration certificate is issued electronically and should be checked for correctness. The ® symbol can only be used once the trade mark is registered in South Africa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the electronic certificate for errors and only begin using ® after registration. Use TM prior to registration to indicate claim of trade mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal and restoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade mark registrations are renewable in 10-year intervals, calculated from the date of application (not date of registration). If missed, late renewal can be done within 12 months after expiration upon payment of a late renewal fee. If not renewed, registration may be removed, but may be restored through prescribed restoration procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diary key renewal and restoration deadlines. Tip: diarise important dates to avoid withdrawal or lapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights granted by registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Registering a trade mark grants the owner several rights: the exclusive right to use the trade mark or authorise others to use it; the right to take legal action against anyone using the same or a confusingly similar trade mark; and the right to use the trade mark as security for loans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and leverage enforcement options; consider using registrations as assets/security in commercial transactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of trade mark rights and non-use cancellation
rubrics_metrics.description: The trade mark may be renewed indefinitely on application for subsequent 10-year periods. If the trade mark is not used in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered for five years or longer after registration, any interested person may apply for cancellation of the registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain use evidencing continuous use to avoid vulnerability to non-use cancellation; renew on time to preserve rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of a well-known trade mark (unregistered)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unregistered marks get protection only if classified as well-known under the Paris Convention; these provisions allow the proprietor of an unregistered well-known mark to oppose any application and/or restrain use of a mark which reproduces, imitates, or translates the well-known mark where use is likely to cause deception or confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you claim well-known status, be prepared to prove reputation/recognition; monitor filings that may conflict with a well-known mark and act during opposition phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright definition and governing statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright is a legal right that protects original creative and artistic works and gives the owner the right to control and profit from their work and to stop unauthorised use. Copyright in South Africa is governed by the Copyright Act, 98 of 1978 (and amendments), the Registration of Copyright in Cinematograph Films Act, 62 of 1977, and related regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the listed Acts and related regulations when advising clients on copyright matters and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration not required for copyright subsistence
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike other statutory IPRs, registration is not required for the subsistence of copyright in South Africa. Copyright subsists automatically once the work is captured in a material form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only cinematograph films may be registered (not compulsory). Because there is no general registration certificate, keep good creation/ownership records to prove subsistence and ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: International arrangements (Berne Convention and TRIPS)
rubrics_metrics.description: South Africa is a signatory to the Berne Convention and the TRIPS Agreement, obliging recognition and protection for works created in other signatory countries; works protected in South Africa are protected in other Berne member states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use international obligations when advising on cross-border protection and qualifications of foreign authors or works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protected works categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The Copyright Act specifies types of works that are protected if original: literary works (novels, scripts, reports, tables), musical works, artistic works (paintings, photographs, architecture, craftsmanship), cinematograph films (including soundtracks and video games), sound recordings, broadcasts, programme-carrying signals, published editions (typographical arrangement), and computer programs (set of instructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correctly identify the category as rights, duration, authorship and exceptions differ by type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of correctly classifying a work
rubrics_metrics.description: If a work cannot be classified within one of the specified types, it is not protected under South African copyright law. Certain aspects of copyright differ based on the type identified (authorship, ownership, duration, exceptions, permitted use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully identify and classify a work to determine scope of protection and applicable rules; misclassification can jeopardise rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: work must be a protected type
rubrics_metrics.description: To subsist, the work must be of a type eligible for copyright protection under the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm the work fits one of the enumerated categories before advising on copyright claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: originality
rubrics_metrics.description: The work must be the product of the creator’s own efforts and skills and not copied from other sources; it does not have to be inventive or new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate evidence of independent creation and avoid reliance on mere ideas; focus on expression rather than novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: material form (fixation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright does not subsist in an idea or concept alone; the work must be written or otherwise reduced to a material form, except broadcasts (become eligible when broadcast) and programme-carrying signals (when transmitted by satellite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure works are fixed/recorded; advise clients to preserve tangible copies or recordings to prove subsistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: author is a 'qualified person'
rubrics_metrics.description: Author (individual) must be a South African citizen, domiciled or resident in South Africa; for juristic persons, an entity incorporated under South African law. Foreign persons from Berne Convention countries are recognised as 'qualified persons'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check author qualification to determine applicable rules; if not qualified, consider 'first publication' rules for protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: First publication rules for non-qualified authors
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author is not a qualified person, for literary/musical/artistic works, sound recordings, cinematograph films, published editions or computer programs, the work must have been first published in South Africa or a Berne member state. For cinematograph films/broadcasts/computer programmes, additional conditions (made in the Republic or emitted from the Republic) apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advising foreign authors, verify first publication location to confirm protection in South Africa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship and ownership general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The author (creator) is the owner of the copyright; in works of joint authorship, copyright is owned collectively by co-authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document contributions and agreements among co-authors to avoid disputes about joint ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioned works ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: For commissioned works paid in money (other than certain exceptions like portraits, gravures, cinematograph films or sound recordings), the author remains the owner unless copyright is assigned in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When commissioning creative work, ensure a written assignment transfers copyright to the commissioning party if that is the commercial intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course and scope of employment (works made in employment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the work is made during the course and scope of employment under a contract of service or apprenticeship, the employer is the initial owner of the copyright, unless the employment/apprenticeship agreement excludes this provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check employment contracts for clear ownership clauses; include IP assignment or licence terms explicitly where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works made for publication in magazines/newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: For works made for publication in a magazine or newspaper, the proprietor of the newspaper or magazine is the initial owner of the work for the purpose of being published, but in all other respects copyright vests with the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiate and record rights for first publication and other exploitations separately in publishing agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: State works ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a work is made by or under the control of the state or an international organisation, the state or such international organisation owns the copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess state contracts and procurement terms to determine ownership and rights to use or reproduce state works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of subsistence and ownership (recordkeeping)
rubrics_metrics.description: As there is no general certificate of registration for copyright works, you need to prove the subsistence of copyright and rights of ownership; therefore keep proper records surrounding creation, updating or acquisition of any copyright work. Registration of a cinematograph film alleviates the burden of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise clients to keep dated drafts, files, contracts, emails, source files and other documentary evidence to establish creation date and ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration depends on type: literary, artistic and musical works are protected for the lifetime of the author plus 50 years from the end of the year in which the author dies. Other works are protected for 50 years after the work is made available to the public, published, or made; State works 50 years from the end of the year first published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use duration rules when clearing rights and advising on expiry of protection; note Berne/TRIPS set minimums and other jurisdictions may extend to 70 years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic rights (copyright owner monopoly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright grants the owner the exclusive right to do or authorise others to perform restricted acts, primarily relating to reproduction or adaptation of the work. The Copyright Act details restricted acts by category of work which are within the monopoly of the copyright owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which restricted acts apply to the particular category of work and advise on licensing/permission required for third-party uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The author retains rights of paternity (to claim authorship) and integrity (to object to distortion, mutilation, or modification prejudicial to reputation), even when the author does not own the copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve moral rights considerations in assignments and licences; authors may enforce these rights separately from economic rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer of copyright (formalities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright is a form of movable property and must be assigned in writing, licensed, transmitted by will or testament, or by operation of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure assignments/licenses are in writing and clearly identify the work being assigned; TIP: assignment must be in writing and signed on behalf of assignor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neighbouring rights — performers’ protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Neighbouring rights, specifically performers’ protection rights, are governed by the Performers’ Protection Act 11 of 1967. This Act regulates the rights of performers, producers, and broadcasters, offering protection for performances of literary, musical and artistic works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise performers and producers about their rights under the Performers’ Protection Act and related amendments (e.g., needletime rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Needletime royalties and collecting societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Needletime royalties are royalties paid to artists and record companies for the copyright licence to play sound recordings in public. The 2002 amendments introduced needletime rights and a definition for collecting societies; Collecting Societies Regulations of 2006 provide rules for establishment, collection and distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise performers and rights-holders to engage with regulated collecting societies for collection and distribution of royalties; ensure societies meet regulatory requirements.
